response.text:
Tuppence, dressed for her afternoon out, made her way to the Ritz. Tommy had not yet returned — another nail in the coffin of her hopes. She resolved to appeal to Mr. Carter, and was addressing the envelope in Julius Hersheimmer's sitting-room when the door burst open.

"What the hell——" began Julius, then checked himself. "I beg your pardon, Miss Tuppence. Those fools down at the office would have it that Beresford wasn't here any longer. Is that so?"

Tuppence nodded. "You don't know where he is?"

"I? I haven't had one darned word from him since we parted at the depot on Wednesday."

"What depot?"

"Waterloo. Didn't he tell you?"

"I haven't seen him either," said Tuppence impatiently. "Go on."

Tommy had telephoned, Julius explained, told him to hustle, and they had met on the platform with two crooks in sight. Tommy had pressed a ticket into his hand and sent him after the big one — Whittington — while Tommy trailed the other.

"Sit down in that armchair," said Tuppence firmly, "and tell me the whole story with as few fancy turns of speech as possible."

Mr. Hersheimmer obeyed.

He had followed Whittington to Bournemouth, to a hotel, then out at nine o'clock across the cliffs to a big house among the pines. Whittington was admitted; Julius waited in the rain till he was near soaked. Restive at last, he prowled the grounds and noticed a lighted upstairs window with the curtains undrawn, and opposite it a tree that might serve.

"It wasn't so easy, by a long chalk. The rain had made the boughs mighty slippery." But he had climbed, and crawled out along a creaking branch till he could see in. Whittington sat at a table talking emphatically to a woman in nurse's uniform, her back turned. The window was shut; he caught no word. Then Whittington asked her something, and she came across to look out.

"Just then the moon came out from behind the clouds. I was full in the moonlight. The jerk I gave was too much for that rotten old branch. With an almighty crash, down it came, and Julius P. Hersheimmer with it!"

"Oh, Julius," breathed Tuppence, "how exciting! Go on."

He had pitched into soft earth — sprained, not broken — and woke to find a black-bearded little doctor with gold glasses examining him. Julius spun some yarn about a girl and a stern guardian, and finally asked outright for Jane Finn.

"He was sure. No Jane Finn. It laid me out for a space."

He had tried Whittington's name. The doctor knew it at once: Whittington had come down to see one of his nurses — Nurse Edith, his niece. But Whittington had returned to town immediately, and Nurse Edith had left with a patient that very night.

"Say, Miss Tuppence, you're looking mighty pale!"

"It's Tommy. What can have happened to him?"

"Buck up. Maybe they've gone abroad — to Poland, or something."

"He couldn't without passports. Besides, I've seen that man Boris since. He dined with Mrs. Vandemeyer last night."

"Mrs. Who?"

Tuppence related the events of the last two days. Julius's astonishment and admiration were unbounded. "Bully for you! Fancy you a menial." Then, seriously: "But these crooks would as soon croak a girl as a man. I wish you'd keep right out of this."

"Do you think I'm afraid?" said Tuppence indignantly, repressing memories of the steely glitter in Mrs. Vandemeyer's eyes. "Let's think about Tommy. I've written to Mr. Carter."

"Good as far as it goes. But it's for us to get busy. I'll buy a car — a slap-up one — dress as a chauffeur, and hang about outside. If Boris comes, you signal and I trail him."

"Splendid. But he mightn't come for weeks."

"We'll chance that." He rose.

"Where are you going?"

"To buy the car, of course."

"Oh," said Tuppence faintly, "I like Rolls-Royces, but——"

"Sure. What you say goes."

"But you can't at once. People wait ages."

"Little Julius doesn't."

She told him then of Sir James Peel Edgerton — how he had seemed, in an ambiguous lawyer's way, to be warning her. "I wouldn't mind going to him and telling him everything."

Julius negatived it sharply. "We don't want any lawyers mixed up in this. So long."

Thirty-five minutes later he returned and walked her to the window.

"There she is."

"Oh!" said Tuppence reverently, gazing down at the enormous car.

"How did you get it?"

"She was being sent home to some bigwig. I went round to his house. Told him a car like that was worth twenty thousand dollars — and that it was worth fifty thousand to me if he'd get out."

"Well?" said Tuppence, intoxicated.

"Well, he got out, that's all."
